classification.difficultyReason: Standardise contextual measurements, use symmetry and cumulative-table subtraction, and interpret an unusually low height.

content.prompt: A Jack Russell terrier has mean height $28$ cm and standard deviation $0.833$ cm. Assume heights are approximately normally distributed. Use the standard normal table for probabilities, rounding z-scores to 2 decimal places and percentages to 2 decimal places.

children.label: a
children.prompt: What range of heights (to 1 d.p.) would you expect within three standard deviations of the mean?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\mu-3\sigma&=28-3(0.833)\\&=25.501\\\mu+3\sigma&=28+3(0.833)\\&=30.499\end{align*}$$
The expected range is approximately $25.5$ cm to $30.5$ cm, containing about $99.7\%$ of heights under the normal model.

children.label: c
children.prompt: What percentage of dogs are between $27.2$ and $30$ cm tall?

answer.worked:
Let $X$ be a dog's height in centimetres. The endpoint z-scores are
$$\begin{align*}z_{27.2}&=\frac{27.2-28}{0.833}\\&\approx-0.96\\z_{30}&=\frac{30-28}{0.833}\\&\approx2.40\end{align*}$$
Using symmetry and the standard normal table,
$$\begin{align*}P(27.2\le X\le30)&\approx P(-0.96\le Z\le2.40)\\&=P(Z\le2.40)-P(Z\le-0.96)\\&=0.9918-(1-0.8315)\\&=0.8233.\end{align*}$$
Approximately $82.33\%$ of dogs are in this height range.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Would a dog $24$ cm tall be typical? Why?

answer.short: No. Its height is about $4.80$ standard deviations below the mean, well outside the usual three-standard-deviation range.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}z&=\frac{24-28}{0.833}\\&\approx-4.80\end{align*}$$
A height of $24$ cm is about $4.80$ standard deviations below the mean and lies outside the expected range of $25.5$ cm to $30.5$ cm. It would not be typical.
